newsitem.title: USA: UAL Corp sees 1997 as record year.
newsitem.headline: UAL Corp sees 1997 as record year.

text.p: UAL Corp, the parent of United Airlines, said it expects 1997 to be "another record setting year."
It said its 1997 results will benefit from the expected decline in fuel prices, continued capacity growth control throughout the airline industry and moderate growth in the U.S. economy.
Soaring fuel costs added $350 million in costs during 1996, the airline said.
United's recent labor woes, however, remain an unknown variable. Earlier this month, the airline's pilots rejected a wage proposal that offered a 10 percent wage increase over four years.
The airline and the pilots will now submit to binding arbitration. An arbiter can assign wage increases of up to five percent for 1997 and 1998.
A mid-term wage adjustment was included as a provision of the pilots' 1994 employee-ownership agreement (ESOP).
United's mechanics also recently rejected a wage proposal.
United said it expects its employee-ownership plan to remain successful despite the recent clash with labor.

"The ESOP has been successful so far and we are counting on continued support of the employees of this company and continued success of the ESOP," said John Edwardson, United's president and chief operating officer.
Edwardson said the ESOP started as a way to align the "expectations and relationships of labor and shareholders."
"We still think it is possible and it's way too early to declare defeat," Edwardson said.
United's management also denied that the clash with the pilots is a sign of deep cultural problems at the airline.

"This is not a culture issue; it is a money issue. It is compensation. And that is the only thing we think it is. The (question) is what will pilots' compensation be at the year 2000?" Edwardson said.
United said it remains willing to listen and address issues with the pilots.
